existing.title: Gabbard Revokes Clearances of 37 Intelligence Officials, Accidentally Exposes CIA Undercover Officer
existing.description_short: Gabbard Revokes Clearances of 37 Intelligence Officials, Accidentally Exposes CIA Undercover Officer
existing.description_long: On August 19, 2025, Director of National Intelligence Tulsi Gabbard revoked the security clearances of 37 current and former national security officials via memo, accusing them without evidence of politicization or weaponization of intelligence. Targeted individuals included career analysts involved in the 2017 intelligence community assessment that Russia interfered in the 2016 election on Trump's behalf, as well as members of Biden's National Security Council. Critically, Gabbard's office failed to coordinate the action with other intelligence agencies. The publicly released list inadvertently exposed the identity of a CIA employee who was undercover and scheduled to take up a post abroad—a potentially career-ending and life-threatening error. NBC News reported September 25, 2025 that the mass revocations also blindsided the Justice Department, which was building a criminal case against former CIA Director John Brennan—and that Gabbard's action labeled potential witnesses as treasonous, undermining the prosecution. CIA Director John Ratcliffe was reportedly furious at the lack of coordination. Legal experts said the move would complicate any future national security prosecutions.

input.original_title: Trump Broad Assertion of Inherent Presidential Power to Override Federal Law

existing.title: Trump Broad Assertion of Inherent Presidential Power to Override Federal Law
existing.description_short: Trump Broad Assertion of Inherent Presidential Power to Override Federal Law
existing.description_long: Across dozens of executive orders issued in January and February 2025, legal scholars Adam Cox and Trevor Morrison documented that Trump was asserting an unprecedented constitutional theory: that the president holds inherent authority to override, disregard, or suspend Acts of Congress when they conflict with his policy agenda. The orders covered immigration, TikTok, energy, birthright citizenship, and more — each relying on claims of inherent executive power that went beyond existing statutes or directly contradicted them. In the TikTok order, Trump instructed the Attorney General not to enforce an Act of Congress for 75 days because the law interfered with his ability to act. In immigration orders, Trump claimed invasion authority allowed him to suspend the entire immigration statutory code. Stanford Law Review published an analysis in July 2025 finding the administration had advanced practical and statutory arguments inflected with constitutional considerations suggesting Article II gave the president a preclusive presidential impoundment prerogative. Courts repeatedly rejected the theory while acknowledging the Supreme Court had not yet rendered a definitive ruling.

The systematic funding elimination targeted sanctuary jurisdictions that had policies 'prohibiting or limiting local law enforcement from taking steps to facilitate deportations,' including cities that declined to hold people in jail longer than legally required in response to ICE detainer requests or refused to provide citizenship information about individuals in custody. Trump's sanctuary city punishment violated federal principles of local autonomy by using funding coercion to force local governments to become immigration enforcement agents, threatening to withhold 'food, shelter, healthcare services, legal services, and transportation' funding that served entire communities rather than just immigrant populations. The comprehensive defunding represented what immigration advocates called 'weaponization of federal resources' to compel local participation in mass deportation operations regardless of community safety concerns, constitutional protections, or local democratic decisions about law enforcement priorities and resource allocation. The White House gained 'dangerously broad discretion' in defining affected programs while jurisdictions faced losing billions in federal grants that supported essential public services including education, disaster response, infrastructure, and public health programs that benefited all residents regardless of immigration status. The sanctuary city targeting demonstrated Trump's strategy to overcome local resistance to mass deportations by creating financial pressure that forced communities to choose between maintaining humanitarian policies and receiving federal resources necessary for basic government operations and constituent services.

The campaign illustrated how Trump's blanket alignment with the crypto industry transformed presidential clemency into a transactional commodity.

The systematic targeting included Colombian nationals, creating diplomatic tensions when foreign governments pushed back against deportation flights.

existing.title: Trans Prisoners Transferred to Wrong-Gender Facilities
existing.description_short: Trans Prisoners Transferred to Wrong-Gender Facilities
existing.description_long: EO 14168, signed January 20, 2025, directed the Attorney General to ensure 'males are not detained in women's prisons' and prohibited federal funds from covering gender-affirming care for inmates, immediately disrupting established Bureau of Prisons (BOP) protocols. A February 21, 2025 BOP memo ordered staff to refer to inmates by pronouns 'corresponding to their biological sex' and banned gender-affirming clothing, cosmetics, and wigs; a second memo one week later banned hormone therapy and surgeries. U.S. District Judge Royce Lamberth issued multiple emergency injunctions beginning February 4, 2025, blocking transfers of named plaintiffs, but a DOJ official on February 18 directed BOP to begin moving all remaining transgender women to men's facilities not covered by the injunctions. An internal BOP memo obtained by the Marshall Project confirmed six transgender women and one transgender man were moved to facilities inconsistent with their gender identity. Incarcerated women who were transferred reported living in constant fear of sexual assault in men's prisons.
